content: The Capital Area Food Bank is a member of America's Second Harvest and serves the local community not only by providing food but also by offering nutritional education. This dual mission has earned it recognition, with Washingtonian magazine naming it one of the top twenty charities in the region. The food bank relies heavily on the support of local volunteers, with over 12,000 individuals annually contributing their time to tasks such as sorting food, teaching classes, and performing other essential duties. The Capital Area Food Bank was established on January 15, 1980, coinciding with Martin Luther King Jr.'s fifty-first birthday. Before its founding, the primary source of assistance for hungry residents in the city was the U.S. government's Food Stamp Program. However, planned cutbacks to the program in the early 1980s prompted the creation of the food bank by two local organizations: the United Planning Organization and the Interfaith Conference of Metropolitan Washington. In its first year, the food bank provided food to nearly 100 organizations and distributed approximately 1,540 pounds (700 kilograms) of food each month. Throughout the 1980s, the food bank expanded its operations, forming partnerships with corporations such as The Washington Post. By 1998, it had opened an additional warehouse in Lorton, Virginia, to meet the needs of Northern Virginia residents. The food bank's facilities have grown significantly, with its current 48,000-square-foot warehouse being more than three times the size of its original 14,000-square-foot space. In 1981, the food bank processed just over one million pounds (460,000 kilograms) of food. By 2005, it was distributing over 20 million pounds (9 million kilograms) of food annually to more than 275,000 people, making it the largest food bank in the area. Due to its proximity to the U.S. government, the Capital Area Food Bank has attracted visits from prominent politicians. For example, President George H.W. Bush famously banned broccoli from the White House and Air Force One, leading to an estimated ten tons of broccoli being sent to the White House, which Barbara Bush subsequently donated to the food bank. That same year, President Bush visited the food bank and incorporated it into his Points of Light Foundation. On Inauguration Day in 1993, over 35,000 cans of food, including one from Tipper Gore, were collected for the food bank. President Bill Clinton visited the food bank in 1999 to volunteer, and President George W. Bush followed suit in 2002. First Lady Laura Bush also visited the food bank to encourage Americans to engage in charitable activities. Other politicians have supported the food bank through donations or by promoting its mission, with the organization receiving $3 million in federal funding to support its efforts.
